Battle of Kursk. The Battle of Kursk was the largest tank engagement in history, fought in July and August 1943 in southern Russia over a bulging Soviet salient known as the Kursk Bulge. German forces under Erich von Manstein and Walter Model launched Operation Citadel to pinch off and destroy the salient. But Soviet forces under Georgy Zhukov had anticipated the offensive and prepared multiple defensive lines with thousands of tanks and guns. The Soviets repulsed the German attacks and counterattacked, pushing German forces west and sealing Germany's fate on the Eastern Front. After Kursk, Germany would never again mount a major offensive in the East.

The Kursk Salient was a Soviet bulge in the front line south of Moscow. German commanders believed destroying it would regain momentum lost at Stalingrad. Operation Citadel was to be a double pincer with Army Group South under Erich von Manstein attacking from the south and Army Group Center under Walter Model from the north. The Soviets learned of the offensive plan in advance through the Lucy spy ring and fortified the salient with seven defensive belts, thousands of anti-tank guns, and massed reserves.

German forces attacked on July 5. Model's northern offensive gained little ground against Soviet defenses. Manstein's southern pincer advanced twenty-five miles but was blunted by Soviet reserves. Soviet Fifth Guards Tank Army under Pavel Rotmistrov delivered massive counterattacks with fierce tank and anti-tank duels engulfing the salient, notably at Prokhorovka on July 12. By July 12, German forces called off the offensive as losses were crippling and German resources could not be replenished, whereas Soviet production was surging.

The Soviets launched their own offensives, pushing German forces west. By August, the Kursk Salient was eliminated in Soviet favor and Soviet armies advanced hundreds of miles. German losses in men, tanks, and aircraft were catastrophic and irreplaceable. Germany abandoned hopes of regaining the initiative in the East. Kursk marked the final strategic shift when the Soviet Union would now dictate the pace of war in Eastern Europe.
